That depends on a lot of things, including what we found (scum on Mars vs. hyper-advanced aliens coming here), and where we found them (still on another planet, e.g. data from a rover, or coming here). Otherwise the question is too vague.

That said, I think that, assuming it wasn't on our door step, it would lead to a somewhat time-limited, but real, additional expenditure on NASA and the space program, particularly if it were intelligent life. In fact, if it were intelligent life I believe it would boost, to some extent, cooperation between countries, albeit it would mostly be in the interests of hoping to attain sufficient knowledge and weaponry to counter the aliens should they turn out to be hostile. If it was Mars scum, it would be a lot less profound, but it would still have a noticeable increase in NASA's budget. Long-term it would probably have a lasting effect, but it would probably push a manned Martian mission back, because they'd want to make sure we wouldn't kill Mars and Mars wouldn't kill us by mistake. There would need to be a lot more probing and scientific analysis. This would become considerably easier if we had some sort of advanced spaceflight drive. I also think the assertion that religion would implode is completely wrong - there would be a few fundamental extremists with brains that would break, but for the most part they'd shrug, say God created life on other planets, too, and go on with their lives. Pope Francis already said that he'd baptize an alien.

Probably the situation that would be most difficult to predict would be, say, if we somehow detected a Dyson sphere. So we know aliens are probably out there with highly advanced technology, but either don't know or don't care about us... NOW what? Other than doing what we can to prevent additional broadcasts from going out and attempting to funnel funds towards spaceflight and space-based weaponry, I'm hard pressed to figure out what else would happen. Religion probably wouldn't change all that much. Ironically the unknowns of this scenario might be deeply disturbing in terms of general security, and might lead to better international cooperation... though I doubt it would do much to "bury the hatchet" so much as be prepared for a possible invasion at some point in the future, and eventually that effect might well deteriorate as well.

Just some thoughts off the top of my head - as I said the question is very vague, and it is also extremely complicated in and of itself.

I've always considered Bohemian Rhapsody to be the apex of rock songwriting and performance, even when I was just a kid. It was just so BIG. Freddie's piano and vocals, Brian May's iconic guitar solo, the operatic section, and Roger Taylor's impossibly high c#6 "MEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE!" I always wanted to play it, because to me, being able to play it would mean that I was a REAL musician. I was a big BIG fan of Queen, and Bohemian Rhapsody to me was like a holy thing, I held it in such high reverence that if I was going to play it, it had to be PERFECT. I never seemed to feel quite capable of the task, so eventually I just shelved the idea, and went about my business. That was about 14 years ago.

Last month, I was fooling around on the piano, not really trying to do anything but get better (Piano is my worst instrument by far). And I just kind of... started. The first few notes just clumsily spilled out, but the second time around it got a little better, and the third... and then it hit me. I'm playing freaking Bohemian Rhapsody. On my WORST instrument... can I play it on my best? So I grabbed a guitar and played Brian May's solo. Holy crap. I can do this. If I can sing the harmonies, I can do this.

Three weeks, almost 400 vocal takes later, and one wife driven crazy by my new temporary obsession, I finally felt satisfied with the end result. So... here it is, for Voat's approval.
